new_misconceptions.message: When you reach x² − 2x = 0, dividing both sides by x loses the solution x = 0 — instead, factorise as x(x − 2) = 0 to find both values.
With a line and a curve you need to set them equal (substitute y = 2x − 3 into y = x² − 3) rather than subtracting one equation from the other, which only works when both equations are linear.
After factorising x(x − 2) = 0 you get two solutions — remember x = 0 is a valid answer as well as x = 2, so pair each x-value with its y-value to give both coordinate pairs.
Finding x = 0 and x = 2 is only half the answer — substitute each back into y = 2x − 3 to get the full coordinate pairs (0, −3) and (2, 1).

rationale: The original quadratic y = x² − 4 paired with y = 2x − 3 gives irrational intersections (x = 1 ± √2); neither stored solution x = −1 or x = 1 satisfies either equation. Stored solutions sum to 0, but with a sloped linear equation y = 2x − 3 the intersection x-values must sum to 2 (the linear coefficient), so no slope-1 or slope-2 line can yield roots ± 1 against a monic x² + c quadratic. The minimal one-constant repair is −4 → −3: y = x² − 3 gives 2x − 3 = x² − 3 → x² − 2x = 0 → x(x − 2) = 0, yielding clean integer solutions x = 0 (y = −3) and x = 2 (y = 1). New solutions set to [0, 2].
